summary.text: Assuming the claimed tail identity, \(b_s=a_{3773+s}+1\) obeys the Fibonacci recurrence; modular computations of the initial terms and relevant Fibonacci numbers modulo \(p=195318521017\) then show that \(p\) divides both \(a_{249580077006}\) and \(a_{249580077007}\). At the next index, with \(g\) their gcd and \(r=(a_{249580077006}+a_{249580077007})/g\), the two recurrence expressions force \((g-1)(r-1)=0\); but \(g\ge p>1\) gives \(r=1\), hence \(g\) equals the sum of two positive terms, contradicting that a gcd is at most either term.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\]
where
\[
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
The quotient is an integer because the gcd divides both summands.

We will disprove the conjecture by showing that even its first asserted identity,
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}, \tag{1}
\]
cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Consequently, the stronger assertion that all three displayed identities hold for every such \(n\) is false.

All terms of the sequence are positive. Indeed, \(a_1=a_2=1\). If two consecutive terms are positive, then their gcd is positive, and the next term is the sum of this positive gcd and a nonnegative integer. Thus, inductively,
\[
a_n\geq1\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{2}
\]

We first record the finite and modular computations used below. Set
\[
p=195318521017.
\]
A direct finite calculation from the defining recurrence gives
\[
 a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod p,
 \qquad
 a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p. \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this calculation is performed by maintaining the exact pair of consecutive integers, not merely their residues: begin with \((x,y)=(1,1)=(a_1,a_2)\), and for each \(k=3,4,\ldots,3774\), replace
\[
(x,y)\longmapsto
\left(y,\ d+\frac{x+y}{d}\right),
\qquad d=\gcd(x,y).
\]
After the replacement indexed by \(k\), the pair is \((a_{k-1},a_k)\). Reducing the last two required outputs modulo \(p\) yields (3). As useful check values near the end of this finite calculation, one obtains
\[
 a_{3772}\equiv21827756562,
 \quad a_{3773}\equiv77940394258,
 \quad a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p;
\]
the gcd used in producing \(a_{3773}\) is \(13\), and the gcd used in producing \(a_{3774}\) is \(1\). Only the last two residues in (3) are needed in the proof.

We will also need three large-index Fibonacci residues. Write \(F_0=0,F_1=1\), and \(F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n\). The standard fast-doubling identities are
\[
F_{2k}=F_k(2F_{k+1}-F_k),
\qquad
F_{2k+1}=F_k^2+F_{k+1}^2. \tag{4}
\]
Thus a pair \((F_k,F_{k+1})\) determines the corresponding pair at indices \(2k\) or \(2k+1\). Starting from \((F_0,F_1)=(0,1)\), processing the binary digits of an index, and reducing after each use of (4), gives all needed residues without constructing the enormous Fibonacci numbers themselves. Here
\[
249580073232=(11101000011100001000011011000100010000)_2.
\]
The resulting pairs modulo \(p\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
(F_{249580073232},F_{249580073233})
  &\equiv(117378126758,21827756563),\\
(F_{249580073233},F_{249580073234})
  &\equiv(21827756563,139205883321)
\end{aligned}
\pmod p. \tag{5}
\]
These are finite modular computations using (4); the overlap of the two pairs also checks the common middle residue.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the conjecture holds for every \(n\geq3775\). In particular, (1) holds for every such \(n\).

Define a shifted sequence
\[
c_s=a_{3773+s}+1\qquad(s\geq0).
\]
Applying (1) at \(n=3775+s\) gives
\[
a_{3775+s}=1+a_{3774+s}+a_{3773+s}.
\]
Adding \(1\) and using the definition of \(c_s\), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{s+2}
 &=a_{3775+s}+1\\
 &=2+a_{3774+s}+a_{3773+s}\\
 &=(a_{3774+s}+1)+(a_{3773+s}+1)\\
 &=c_{s+1}+c_s.
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
Thus \((c_s)\) satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence.

For any sequence satisfying (6), induction gives
\[
c_{m+1}=F_{m+1}c_1+F_mc_0, \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
c_{m+2}=F_{m+2}c_1+F_{m+1}c_0. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, for \(m=0\), (7) says \(c_1=F_1c_1+F_0c_0\), and (8) says \(c_2=F_2c_1+F_1c_0=c_1+c_0\). If the two formulas hold at one stage, adding the two consecutive expressions and using both the recurrence for \(c\) and that for \(F\) gives the next expression. This proves (7) and (8) for all \(m\geq0\).

In the present case,
\[
c_0=a_{3773}+1,
\qquad
c_1=a_{3774}+1.
\]
By (3),
\[
c_0\equiv77940394259,
\qquad
c_1\equiv99768150822
\pmod p. \tag{9}
\]
Take
\[
m=249580073232.
\]
Then
\[
3773+(m+1)=249580077006,
\qquad
3773+(m+2)=249580077007. \tag{10}
\]
Using (7), (5), and (9), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{249580077006}+1
  &=c_{m+1}\\
  &=F_{m+1}c_1+F_mc_0\\
  &\equiv
21827756563\cdot99768150822
 +117378126758\cdot77940394259
\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
The integer on the last line is
\[
11326212385784681827108
 =57988419771\,p+1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a_{249580077006}+1\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence
\[
p\mid a_{249580077006}. \tag{11}
\]

Similarly, (8), (5), and (9) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{249580077007}+1
  &=c_{m+2}\\
  &=F_{m+2}c_1+F_{m+1}c_0\\
  &\equiv
139205883321\cdot99768150822
 +21827756563\cdot77940394259
\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the last integer equals
\[
15589577514788957011679
 =79816176334\,p+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
a_{249580077007}+1\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so
\[
p\mid a_{249580077007}. \tag{12}
\]

We now compare the conjectured recurrence with the actual defining recurrence at
\[
n_0=249580077008.
\]
Put
\[
x=a_{249580077007},
\qquad
y=a_{249580077006},
\qquad
g=\gcd(x,y).
\]
By (11) and (12), \(p\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), and therefore
\[
p\mid g. \tag{13}
\]
In particular, because \(p>1\),
\[
g>1. \tag{14}
\]
Also, by positivity (2), \(x,y\geq1\), so \(g>0\). Since \(g\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), it divides \(x+y\). Define
\[
r=\frac{x+y}{g}.
\]
Then
\[
x+y=gr. \tag{15}
\]

The actual definition of the sequence at \(n_0\) says
\[
a_{n_0}=g+r. \tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, the conjectured identity (1), which by assumption applies at \(n_0\), says
\[
a_{n_0}=1+x+y=1+gr. \tag{17}
\]
Comparing (16) and (17),
\[
g+r=1+gr.
\]
Rearranging gives
\[
(g-1)(r-1)=0. \tag{18}
\]
There are now two cases. If \(g-1=0\), then \(g=1\), contradicting (14). Hence the other factor in (18) must vanish, and
\[
r=1. \tag{19}
\]
Equations (15) and (19) then imply
\[
g=x+y. \tag{20}
\]
But a gcd divides \(x\); since \(x>0\), this gives \(g\leq x\). At the same time, \(y\geq1\), so
\[
x+y>x.
\]
Together with (20), this says \(g>x\), contradicting \(g\leq x\).

This contradiction arose solely from assuming that the first proposed formula holds for every \(n\geq3775\). Thus that formula must fail at some index between \(3775\) and \(249580077008\) (at the latest, the argument reaches a contradiction at the latter index). Therefore it is impossible that, for every \(n\geq3775\), all three conjectured formulas
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2},
\qquad
a_n=2a_{n-1}-a_{n-3},
\]
and
\[
a_n=(a_{3774}+1)F_{n-3772}-(a_{3772}+1)F_{n-3774}-1
\]
hold simultaneously. The OEIS conjecture is false.
